title: Sage leaf infusion for digestion
subtitle: A bitter-tonic cup after a heavy meal
excerpt: A hot infusion of dried sage leaf, traditionally taken after a heavy or rich meal to settle the stomach and ease trapped wind. One teaspoon of dried leaf steeped covered for five to seven minutes makes a single cup with a camphor-edged, faintly bitter flavour. Not for long-term daily use.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), sage entry: documents the digestive use of sage leaf infusion and the traditional after-meal cup. Nicholas Culpeper, The English Physician (1652), sage entry: records use for digestion and 'helping weak stomach'. British Herbal Pharmacopoeia (1983), sage leaf monograph: dosing reference for dried herb infusion. EMA HMPC monograph on Salviae officinalis folium (2016): safety guidance on thujone content and duration limits.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Dried sage stores 12 months in a tin or sealed jar away from light and heat. Prepare each cup fresh.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Prepare fresh for each dose. Do not store the brewed infusion.

glossaryTerms.definition: A preparation made by pouring just-boiled water over leaves or flowers and steeping them covered, so the volatile oils stay in the cup rather than escaping with the steam.
A herb with a noticeably bitter taste, traditionally used before or after meals to stimulate digestive secretions and support the stomach's own processes.

content.text: Sage leaf infusion is a hot, faintly bitter cup made from dried garden sage steeped in just-boiled water. Western herbalists have long reached for it after a heavy or fatty meal, for flatulence, and for a sluggish stomach that sits uncomfortably after eating. The cup is thin and clear with a camphor-herbal smell; the flavour is dry and faintly astringent. One teaspoon of dried leaf per cup steeped covered for five to seven minutes is the standard preparation, and the dried leaf keeps well for a year in a sealed tin.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body:
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.

Sage contains thujone, a volatile oil that accumulates with prolonged use. Do not take sage leaf infusion at therapeutic dose daily for more than two to three weeks without a break. Culinary use of sage in cooking carries no significant risk; it is the concentrated daily tea that the thujone caution applies to.

Pregnancy: do not use this infusion at therapeutic dose in pregnancy. Culinary amounts of sage in cooking are not the same as a daily medicinal cup.

Breastfeeding: sage is the traditional milk-suppressing herb and actively reduces milk supply. Do not take this infusion during established breastfeeding unless the aim is weaning.

Paediatric use is not adult-divided-by-half. Consult a herbalist who specialises in children's herbal medicine, or a paediatric doctor, before using any herbal preparation in children under twelve.

content.text: Put 1 teaspoon of dried sage leaf into a teapot or a cup with a tight-fitting lid.
Pour over 200 ml of water that has just come off the boil. Put the lid on immediately to keep the aromatic oils in.
Steep covered for 5 to 7 minutes. The water will be pale greenish-gold and smell strongly of sage when you lift the lid.
Strain through a sieve into a cup and drink warm.

One cup (200 ml) taken after a meal, up to twice a day. For a short course after a period of rich or heavy eating: up to two to three weeks. Then take a break of equal length before another course. Do not drink sage tea daily as a long-term habit owing to the thujone content.
Prepare each cup fresh. Dried sage leaf stores in a sealed tin or glass jar away from light and heat for up to 12 months. Discard when the smell fades significantly.
When not to use this remedy
See a doctor for indigestion that wakes you at night, comes with unexplained weight loss. Painful swallowing, vomiting, black or tarry stools, or chest pain that radiates to the arm or jaw.

Do not use this infusion in pregnancy, during established breastfeeding, or for more than two to three weeks continuously. Anyone with epilepsy should avoid concentrated sage preparations, as thujone has been linked to lowering the seizure threshold at high doses.

items.symptom: Infusion tastes very bitter or harsh
items.cause: Steeped too long or used too much dried herb
items.fix: Keep to 5 to 7 minutes and 1 level teaspoon. Over-steeping extracts more tannins and makes the cup unpleasantly astringent.

items.cause: Dried sage has lost its volatile oil through age or poor storage
items.fix: Replace your dried sage. Properly stored dried sage should smell strongly and clearly herbal when rubbed between the fingers.
